newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Tsumeb manager still trapped by strikers.
newsitem.headline: Tsumeb manager still trapped by strikers.

text.p: A mine manager and his wife besieged in their home by striking copper miners in Namibia on Wednesday began their second day as hostages, despite a bid by the Nambian government to end the confrontation.
The bitter six-week old dispute at Tsumeb Corp Ltd (TCL) took a violent twist when armed strikers gained control of the group's three mines and surrounded manager Tony de Beer's house.
"He is still at his house and cannot leave his home," a spokesman for owners Gold Fields Namibia Ltd told Reuters by telephone from Namibia.
Namibian government ministers on Tuesday visited Tsumeb's Otjihase mine to ask the strikers to put down their weapons -- which include shotguns, pangas (long knives), knobkerries (clubs) and whips.

But the efforts by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Mines had not yet succeeded and they were set to visit Tsumeb's other two mines -- Kombat and Tsumeb -- on Wednesday morning, the spokesman said.
The siege began on Monday night as strikers from the Mineworkers' Union of Namibia tried to enter de Beer's house, but were driven back by police and a warning shot from de Beers.
Strikers returned on Tuesday morning and have camped outside the property since then.
Mediation efforts to halt the strike broke down last Thursday and violent protest flared over the weekend injuring eight people in clashes between strikers and police.
The spokesman said there had been no more violent clashes since Monday, but that the miners were still in control of all three mines. "They have control of all the operations," he said.
He added that the situation was on a knife-edge.
"The situation is terribly, terribly tense," he said.

The strike over pay began with TCL offering a seven percent rise and the union wanting 14.5 percent. A new pay offer is to be put forward by Friday aimed at settling the dispute or, at least, starting mediation again.
Tsumeb mines and smelters have been shut down since August 23 when MUN members began to strike.
The strike is costing TCL some 80 tonnes a day in lost copper production and a similar amount in lost lead.
TCL produced just under 30,000 tonnes of blister copper last year and 27,000 tonnes of lead. Most of the lead was produced from bought-in material while copper output was from TCL mines.
